# Large multi-feature tasks

When a request is big — multiple features, or a large ask that naturally splits into independent
pieces of work — do not implement it as one monolithic pass. Split it into separate commits, one
per feature/unit of work, and drive each unit through this graph-engineering framework using the
Agent tool:

```
Task -> Planner -> Worker -> [Reviewer 1, Reviewer 2, ... Reviewer N] -> Synthesise -> Pass?
                     ^                                                        |
                     |-------------------- feedback (no) ---------------------|
                                                                               |
                                                                          (yes) -> commit -> next unit
```

- **Planner**: breaks the overall ask into an ordered list of commit-sized units of work (a
  Plan Reviewer can review the plan itself before execution starts; route its feedback back to
  the Planner and send a summary of plan feedback to the user).
- **Worker**: a resident agent (kept alive across the reviewer round for a given unit) that
  implements one unit of work.
- **Reviewers (1..N)**: spawn multiple reviewer agents in parallel against the Worker's output —
  e.g. correctness, simplification/efficiency, and test coverage as separate reviewer passes.
  These can be ephemeral (fresh agent per round).
- **Synthesise**: reconcile the reviewers' findings into one set of required changes.
- **Pass? gate**: if synthesised feedback has no blocking issues, finalize and commit that unit
  with its own commit message, then move to the next planned unit. If it fails, send the
  synthesised feedback back to the Worker as another round on the same unit (don't restart from
  the Planner unless the feedback reveals the plan itself was wrong).

Net effect: one commit per feature/unit, each vetted by multiple reviewer passes before it lands,
rather than a single large uncommitted or unreviewed diff at the end.

## Verifying UI work: visual recreation (the main way to verify)

For any unit that changes UI, the primary verification is a **visual recreation**: render the real
components with mock data and look at a screenshot. Typecheck and unit tests are necessary but do not
count as verifying how it looks. Workers should do this before reporting, and I re-do it (or open the
image for the user) when the user asks to see it.

1. Add a **temporary** preview route (e.g. `apps/web/app/zz-preview/page.tsx`) that imports the real
   components and renders them with realistic mock props: populated, empty, capped/failed, long
   names/links. Put context around them (page background, a mock frame for panels/drawers that need a
   session or client state) but never reimplement the component itself.
2. Start the dev server in the background with dummy env vars the app needs to boot (e.g.
   `CONVEX_URL=https://dummy.convex.cloud CONVEX_DEPLOY_KEY=x NEXT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1 bunx next dev -p <port>`),
   wait for "Ready", and `curl` the route for a 200.
3. Screenshot with headless Chrome, not the preview MCP tools (those time out):
   `"/Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome" --headless=new --disable-gpu --hide-scrollbars --force-device-scale-factor=2 --virtual-time-budget=6000 --window-size=<w>,<h> --screenshot=/tmp/<name>.png <url>`
   Take a wide desktop shot and a narrow one. Headless Chrome enforces a minimum window width, so a
   narrow shot can come out horizontally clipped; for true 320px checks render inside a 320px-wide
   iframe or measure element widths, and say so rather than treating clipping as a bug.
4. **Read the PNG** (the Read tool shows images) and actually look at it: hierarchy, spacing, truncation,
   overflow, alignment, tap targets, copy. Report what was seen versus what was not verified
   (hover/focus states, real clipboard/share, animations, Safari-only behavior, the real page behind auth).
5. For the user, `open` the desktop screenshot (copy it to `~/Downloads/<name>.png` first) since they
   can't see tool-output images.
6. **Clean up before committing**: stop the dev server (`pkill -f "next dev -p <port>"`), delete the
   preview route, temp public files and stray `.next` artifacts, and confirm `git status` shows only
   intended changes. Never commit a preview route or mocks.

# Mandatory visual + local-server verification (every agent, every run)

Applies to any task that changes code a user can see or that the running app depends on. No unit of
work is "done" until both of these have happened and been reported:

1. **Run it against the local server.** Start the real dev server (and `npx convex dev` when Convex
   code changed) in this worktree, wait for "Ready", and exercise the changed path end to end: `curl`
   the route for the expected status and hit changed API routes. A passing typecheck/lint/build alone
   does not count.
2. **Verify visually with a screenshot.** Follow the visual-recreation steps above (headless Chrome,
   wide + narrow shot), then Read the PNG and look at it. For pages behind auth, use a temporary
   preview route with mock data. Non-UI changes still get a screenshot of the affected page to prove
   nothing regressed.
3. **Report** what was seen, what was not verified (hover/focus, auth-gated pages, animations), and
   the screenshot path. If the server can't boot (e.g. missing env vars), say so explicitly and fix
   the env first (see below); never claim success without having run it.
4. Clean up (stop the server, delete preview routes/temp files) before committing.

Env vars: each worktree needs its own copy of the gitignored `.env*` files. If `.env.local` is
missing in the current worktree, symlink it from the canonical copy at `~/.config/avian/.env.local`
(`ln -s ~/.config/avian/.env.local .env.local`) before starting the server.

 # AgentBisect
 
-`git bisect` for agent behavior. Give it one bad neatlogs trace; it finds the commit that caused the regression, explains why that commit was written (Entire checkpoints), and ships a verified fix.
+`git bisect` for agent behavior. Give it a failing agent run (or just a known-good and known-bad commit). It finds the commit that broke the behavior, explains why that commit was written, and proves the culprit by reverting it.
 
-Built for neatHack (Oct 10-12, 2026). Status: scaffold. See `hackathon.md` for the build log.
+Built for neatHack (Oct 10-12, 2026).
 
-Setup: `uv sync`, then copy `.env.example` to `.env` and fill in values.
+> **Status of the numbers in this README.** Anything marked `[[RERUN3: ...]]` is a placeholder for the final re-run
+> figures, which live in [`evidence/rerun3-summary.md`](evidence/rerun3-summary.md). Nothing marked that way has been
+> filled in by hand. Everything else cites a file in `evidence/`.
+
+## What it is
+
+Agents regress in ways unit tests do not catch: a refactor changes the unit of a refund amount, a "helpful" change makes the agent cancel orders nobody asked to cancel, a new tool schema quietly doubles token spend. `git bisect` can find the commit, but it needs a deterministic good/bad test, and an LLM agent gives you a noisy one.
+
+AgentBisect supplies that test. It runs the target repo's eval suite at each commit it probes, in an isolated git worktree, with repeats and a calibrated baseline so a flaky run is not mistaken for a regression. Then it bisects.
+
+The demo target is [`support-agent-demo`](https://github.com/jaxsonsprinkles/support-agent-demo): a customer-support agent (pinned Haiku) with mocked tools, 24 eval cases, and a seeded history of regressions written by a separate coding-agent session.
+
+## How it works
+
+1. **Intake.** Start from a neatlogs trace, a neatlogs detection, or a GitHub issue. Intake maps it to an eval case, finds a known-good commit (an earlier passing run of the same case), and records a `RegressionSpec`.
+2. **Failure signatures.** At the bad end, every distinct failing check (for example `call_args:issue_refund.amount`, `must_not_call`, `budget:tokens@order_status`) becomes its own *signature*, and each is bisected separately. One range can hide several regressions; bisecting "the suite fails" would blame whichever commit lands last. A signature that also fails at the good end is a known pre-existing failure, and AgentBisect refuses to bisect it instead of inventing a culprit.
+3. **Plain bisect.** Classic binary search over `git rev-list --first-parent`, with a monotonic probe after convergence that flags "multiple regressions likely" when the history is not clean good-then-bad.
+4. **Smart (weighted) bisect.** A planner ranks the commits in range by how likely each is to be the culprit, then picks the next commit by weighted bisection (split the probability mass, not the commit count) and falls back to plain when the ranking is uninformative. Signals, in order:
+   - **Span divergence**: where the bad run first differs from a good run (a different tool, different arguments, an extra step). See [span divergence](#span-divergence-and-the-fixture-fallback).
+   - **Code impact**: `entire graph impact` finds which commits touched the code behind the divergent tool.
+   - **Entire intent**: each candidate's [Entire](https://entire.io) checkpoint (the prompt and reasoning of the coding session that wrote it). Commits that were *meant* to change the failing area rank higher.
+5. **Median budget checks.** Token and step regressions are judged against a per-case **median** from a one-time calibration run at the good commit (`agentbisect calibrate`), never recalibrated mid-investigation. A run is over budget past 1.5x the case median. Medians, not means, so one slow sample does not move the line.
+6. **Verifier (revert test).** The culprit is only reported with confidence if reverting it at the bad end flips the signature from failing to passing (before and after pass rates are recorded). Revert conflicts, partial reverts and unbuildable trees lower confidence or end as `inconclusive`.
+7. **Explain.** The culprit report quotes the Entire checkpoint (why the commit was written), the semantic diff, and the first span divergence, so the answer is "this commit, written to do X, causes Y", not just a SHA.
+8. **Fixer (upcoming).** A fresh agent that sees only the culprit diff, the stated intent, and the failing evidence (never the planted-regression metadata) proposes a fix that keeps the intent. **Not built yet.** `report --open-pr` is a dry run by default and needs `--confirm-open-pr` to push anything.
+
+Roles, model pins and isolation rules are in [`ROLES.md`](ROLES.md). The agent and judge models are pinned and recorded in every result, and results produced under different pins are never mixed.
+
+### Measured so far
+
+| What | Result | Source |
+|---|---|---|
+| Planner context with the Entire graph vs reading the raw range | 12,869 vs 26,420 tokens (51.3% cut), one investigation | [`evidence/entire-context-savings.md`](evidence/entire-context-savings.md) |
+| Signatures correct on the full-range re-run | `[[RERUN3: N of M correct]]` | [`evidence/rerun3-summary.md`](evidence/rerun3-summary.md) |
+| Eval rounds, smart vs plain, per signature | `[[RERUN3: per-signature rounds table]]` | [`evidence/rerun3-summary.md`](evidence/rerun3-summary.md) |
+| Revert tests passed | `[[RERUN3: n passed of m run]]` | [`evidence/rerun3-summary.md`](evidence/rerun3-summary.md) |
+
+`agentbisect summary <state_dir> --format md` regenerates the per-signature table from saved state.
+
+## Setup
+
+Requirements: Python 3.11 to 3.13 (the neatlogs SDK does not support 3.14), [`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), `git`, and for the full pipeline the `entire` CLI with the `graph` plugin.
+
+```bash
+uv sync
+cp .env.example .env     # NEATLOGS_API_KEY, NEATLOGS_PROJECT_ID, ...
+uv run pytest -q         # fake executors and throwaway git repos; no model or network calls
+```
+
+The target repo needs `evals/cases.jsonl` and the eval CLI contract (`python -m evals run --json --isolate ...`, schema version 1) described in the `support-agent-demo` repo. Clone it next to this one.
+
+Optional pieces:
+
+- **neatlogs CLI** (`npm i -g --prefix ~/.local/neatlogs-cli neatlogs-cli`) for live trace intake, after a one-time `auth login --device`. See `hackathon.md`.
+- **Entire** (`entire enable` in the target repo; `entire plugin install graph`) for checkpoint intent and code impact. Without it the planner falls back to commit messages and plain bisect.
+- **LLM backend.** Either set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, or run on your own logged-in `claude` CLI with `--llm-proxy auto` (personal use, your own login only; see `ROLES.md`). The proxy cannot set temperature, so repeats absorb the extra noise.
+
+## Usage
+
+```bash
+# 1. Calibrate the token baseline once, at the known-good commit
+uv run agentbisect calibrate --repo ../support-agent-demo --good 1b40b27 --llm-proxy auto
+
+# 2. Investigate from a bad trace (or --detection ID, or --issue URL)
+uv run agentbisect investigate --trace <trace-id> --repo ../support-agent-demo \
+    --strategy smart --all-signatures --all-categories --llm-proxy auto
+
+# or skip neatlogs and name the range yourself
+uv run agentbisect investigate --trace <trace-id> --repo ../support-agent-demo \
+    --fixtures path/to/bundle.json --good 1b40b27 --bad 0ecffc0
+
+uv run agentbisect status [ID]          # investigations and their steps
+uv run agentbisect resume ID            # continue after an interruption
+uv run agentbisect compare ID           # plain vs smart: eval rounds and cost
+uv run agentbisect summary --format md  # per-signature results table
+uv run agentbisect report ID            # Markdown + HTML report in evidence/
+```
+
+State lives in `.agentbisect/` (atomic writes, resumable mid-step). Run `uv run agentbisect --help` for all flags.
+
+### Span divergence and the fixture fallback
+
+Live span divergence reads multi-span traces from neatlogs. At the time of writing, those traces finalize as `dlq` with zero spans (see Limitations), so for the demo the same step runs on a **recorded fixture**:
+
+```bash
+uv run python -m agentbisect.fixtures fixtures/divergence/os1-search-help
+```
+
+```
+FIXTURE: recorded from real eval-runner output (tool calls of one case at a good and a bad commit). Not live neatlogs data.
+good local-3b41... (1b40b27...), bad local-5455... (0ecffc0...), case os1
+first divergence: step 1: bad run made an extra step search_help
+```
+
+The fixture is the tool-call sequence of case `os1` ("Where is order 1042?") at `1b40b27` and `0ecffc0`, taken from real `python -m evals run --json` output (Haiku through the llm-proxy). It is always labelled as a fixture, never presented as live neatlogs data. The bad commit is the tip of the range, so the fixture shows where behavior changed (an extra `search_help` step), not which commit caused it. It contains tool-call spans only; model-call spans are not in the runner's report. `agentbisect.fixtures.FixtureDirSource` plugs into the same `TraceSource` interface as the live source, and `--bundle OUT.json` writes the single-file form that `--fixtures` accepts. `record_pair` records new fixtures from two eval reports.
+
+## Limitations
+
+Stated plainly, because the evidence says so:
+
+- **neatlogs span divergence is blocked.** Multi-span traces dead-letter (`finalizationStatus: "dlq"`, `spansCount: 0`) even for a bare two-span script with no model calls; the SDK reports zero export failures. Reported with trace ids in [`evidence/neatlogs-dlq-report.md`](evidence/neatlogs-dlq-report.md). Until it is resolved the planner ranks on code impact and checkpoint intent, and the divergence demo uses the recorded fixture above. The neatlogs read path (`NeatlogsCliSource.spans`) was written against the documented CLI and its real span shape is unverified.
+- **Token-budget signatures are the weak spot.** Every token regression (a new tool schema, an extra "verify with search" rule) inflates every category, so a per-category budget signature tends to blame whichever commit crosses 1.5x last, and its revert test can fail with "multiple regressions likely". Behavioural signatures (wrong arguments, forbidden tool calls) are far more reliable. See `evidence/rerun3-summary.md` for the per-signature outcomes: `[[RERUN3: final correct/incorrect count]]`.
+- **Smart is not always cheaper.** It used fewer eval rounds than plain on behavioural signatures but more on some budget signatures (see the re-run evidence). The planner-context saving is measured on one investigation and one range.
+- **Noisy judge of "bad".** Haiku at non-zero temperature (the proxy cannot set it) is stochastic. Repeats, medians and a confidence band reduce but do not remove this; low-confidence culprits are labelled as such.
+- **Token counts for context savings are bytes/4 estimates**, comparable only within that metric, and the "without graph" side is an estimate, not a second run.
+- **Fixer is not built.** Culprit explanation and the revert test exist; automatic fix generation and fix verification do not.
+- **One target repo.** Everything was exercised against `support-agent-demo`. The eval contract is generic, but nothing else has been tried.
+
+## Repository map
+
+| Path | What |
+|---|---|
+| `agentbisect/intake.py` | trace/detection/issue intake, `TraceSource` (neatlogs CLI and fixture sources) |
+| `agentbisect/runner.py`, `baseline.py` | isolated eval runs, repeats, caching, median-token baseline |
+| `agentbisect/signature.py`, `bisect.py`, `planner.py` | failure signatures, plain and weighted bisect, ranking |
+| `agentbisect/culprit.py`, `verify.py` | Entire intent + diff + divergence, revert test |
+| `agentbisect/fixtures.py`, `fixtures/` | recorded good/bad trace pair for the divergence step |
+| `agentbisect/llm_proxy.py` | Anthropic-compatible proxy over your `claude` login |
+| `evidence/` | reports and re-run summaries |
+| `docs/demo-script.md`, `docs/storyboard.md` | 3-minute demo narration and shot list |
+| `hackathon.md`, `BUILD_LOG.md`, `ROLES.md` | build log, roles and pinning rules |

## boardui
BoardUI is a React + Tailwind CSS v4 design system (Next.js first) with free components and paid Pro components/templates. This server installs component source directly into the user's project — no terminal needed.

Typical flow:
1. In a project without BoardUI, call init_boardui once (installs Tailwind v4 + runtime deps, writes styles/ and utils/).
2. Discover with list_components; read source/props with get_component; get working code with get_usage_examples.
3. Install with install_components — it writes the files and installs npm deps.

Component names are exact — when unsure, call list_components instead of guessing.

## RTL Support

BoardUI supports Arabic, Hebrew, and other right-to-left languages across free components, Pro blocks, and templates. The same source handles RTL and LTR; there is no RTL CLI flag or separate component version.

1. Read get_component and get_usage_examples for the free `direction` item. Install it with install_components (stdio), or write its source and dependencies yourself (read-only HTTP). CLI equivalent: `npx boardui@latest add direction`.
2. Wrap the app with DirectionProvider using an explicit BCP 47 locale: `ar` for Arabic, `he` for Hebrew, `en-US` for English. Set matching `lang` and `dir` on `<html>` for a full-app RTL layout. CSS dir alone does not configure React Aria keyboard navigation, calendars, or portalled menus.

```tsx
import { DirectionProvider } from "@/components/foundations/direction/direction";

export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <html lang="ar" dir="rtl">
      <body>
        <DirectionProvider locale="ar">{children}</DirectionProvider>
      </body>
    </html>
  );
}
```

3. Use logical styles such as ps/pe, ms/me, start/end, and text-start/text-end. Mirror navigation arrows and drawer motion; preserve physical coordinates for charts, canvas, and decorative art. Custom portals should carry `dir={useDirection()}` on their root. Nest DirectionProvider for mixed-language regions.
4. Keep email addresses, URLs, OTP digits, and code LTR; isolate mixed text with bdi or dir=auto. Choose fonts with Arabic or Hebrew coverage and avoid extra letter spacing for Arabic. Translate application labels and accessible names in the application's translation layer; use Intl for dates, numbers, and currencies. Optional `template-copy` supplies TemplateCopyProvider for translating template display copy. Chinese (`zh-CN`) remains LTR.
5. For older installations, refresh the provider, component source, shared dependencies, and global styles. Preserve customizations before using overwrite. Pro updates use the licensed CLI or updated source downloads.

Setup and live Arabic/Hebrew examples: https://www.boardui.com/rtl

Design rules (always apply when writing UI in a BoardUI project): style with BoardUI's semantic Tailwind tokens, never raw palette classes or hex — text via text-text-primary/-secondary/-tertiary, surfaces via bg-background-*-default/-hover, borders via border-border-* and border-separator-border, icons via text-foreground-icon-*. Type uses composite utilities (text-title-2-medium, text-headline-medium, text-body-medium, ...) that set size/weight/line-height together — never rebuild them from text-sm font-medium. Dark mode flips tokens automatically via the .dark class; never hardcode dark: colors. Merge classes with cx() from @/utils/cx (or the utils alias configured in boardui.json); icons from @remixicon/react as component references. init_boardui installs these rules as always-on files (AGENTS.md + .cursor/rules/boardui.mdc) so they survive beyond this session; install_rules adds them to an already initialized project.

Monorepos/custom aliases: put boardui.json next to the destination package's package.json, and pass that package as projectDir. Installs read its paths/aliases and keep npm dependencies in that package. Pass projectDir to get_component and get_usage_examples too for matching source and examples. # Entire graph context savings (measured)

Measured on the first real investigation `6857f0b738` (support-agent-demo, range `2f49adb535`..`f7d82b789e`,
13 commits in range, 13 ranked candidates). Source: `evidence/report-6857f0b738.md` ("Steps and context tokens")
and the saved state `.agentbisect/investigations/6857f0b738.json` (`context_tokens_per_step`, `metrics.planner.context_tokens`);
the `compare-smart` run (`28eee54e3b`) recorded identical numbers.

| context the planner needed | tokens |
|---|---|
| With entire graph + checkpoints (`plan:graph:rank`) | 12,869 |
| Without the graph, reading the raw range (`plan:without_graph`) | 26,420 |
| Saved | 13,551 tokens, **51.3% cut** (12,869 / 26,420 = 0.487) |

## How it was measured

- Tokens are bytes/4 rounded up (`planner.tokens_of_bytes`), not model-reported counts, so compare only within this metric.
- "With graph": every byte the planner actually read while planning, recorded by `Planner._read(...)`: `entire graph impact`
  output to locate impacted code, then the checkpoint intent (or commit message when no checkpoint) of only the commits
  that the graph linked to that code. Logged per phase via `StateStore.log_context_tokens` (label `plan:graph:<phase>`).
- "Without graph" (`Planner._baseline`): what a reader with no graph would have to read to rank the same range: the full
  `git diff good..bad` in bytes, plus the intent text of every commit in range (those actually read counted as-is, the
  rest at the average size of those). Logged as `plan:without_graph`.
- Both numbers are produced in the same planning pass on the same range, so the ratio is like for like.

## Caveats

- One investigation, one range; the saving depends on how much of the range the graph can exclude.
- The "without graph" side is an estimate of the raw diff plus intents, not a second run that read it.
- This is planner context only. It is separate from eval rounds: on this run smart bisect used more eval rounds than plain
  (84 vs 36), which unit U3 addresses.
